segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol and fitted straight (RMS 3 m)); then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (4 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); the sheet corrected by a shift on 3 control points (Yerba Buena Island on the 1949 Oakland West sheet; +74 m E, +213 m N, RMS 44.8 m). The trestle runs straight from the shore, then curves to the ferry terminal.
segments.notes: Ferry trains ran to its end until the Bay Bridge opened to trains in January 1939; from then its land end carried the bridge trains. A 1933 fire is relayed via Wikipedia only.

segments.name: Transbay Terminal loop, San Francisco
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco North 1:24,000 (1950) (23 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). The loop as the 1950 sheet draws it ("KEY SYSTEM"): from the approach, north along the west side to the terminal's west end, through the six-track station facing Mission Street, around the east end and back south. Trains ran counter-clockwise, arriving at the station's east end.

segments.name: San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge, lower deck
segments.method: Joined to bbr-sf-loop at its start; then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco North 1:24,000 (1950) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol and fitted straight (RMS 2 m)); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (8 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (6 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). From Rincon Hill across the bridge's lower deck, through the Yerba Buena Island tunnel, to where the tracks left the bridge on its south side at the Oakland end. The 1946-50 sheets draw the bridge, not the tracks on it; the tracks were on the south half of the lower deck.

segments.name: East Bay approach and yards
segments.method: Joined to bbr-bridge at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (6 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). Along the south side of the bridge approach ("KEY SYSTEM" on the 1949 sheet) past the toll plaza to the East Bay yards, where the Key System's and the Interurban's tracks divided.

segments.name: East Bay yards to the old pier line
segments.method: Joined to bbr-east-approach at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then joined to key-pier at its start. From the East Bay yards over the bridge approach to the north side of the mole ("TRANSIT LINES" on the 1949 sheet), meeting the old pier line.

segments.name: Pier approach and subway to Poplar Junction
segments.method: Joined to key-pier at its start; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (3 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (4 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). From the pier's land end under the Southern Pacific main line (the 1903 subway) to Poplar Junction, along the line the 1949 sheet draws there.

segments.name: Yerba Buena Avenue to San Pablo Avenue
segments.method: Joined to key-trunk-shore at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). Along Yerba Buena Avenue to the station at San Pablo Avenue.

segments.name: San Pablo Avenue to Adeline Street, by Linden Street

lines.summary: Trains from the steamer landing at Donahue, on the Petaluma River, by Petaluma to Santa Rosa (1870), Healdsburg (1871) and Cloverdale (1872).
lines.notes: The company's own returns open Donahue to Santa Rosa on January 1, 1870, before the line was built in the autumn of 1870 (Sonoma County history); the map takes October 1870, when a passenger car was put on to Santa Rosa. Donahue to Petaluma, eight miles along the river, isn't drawn: no map of it has been traced. By 1887 it was a branch, and trains came from Tiburon instead (decision 20 draws this line to 1885, the last date a source shows it running).

running.note: "Line of Road.— Donahue, Cal., to Cloverdale, Cal 56.00 miles", with the steamer "Between Donahue and San Francisco (34 miles)".

lines.summary: The Santa Fe's trains from Chicago and the San Joaquin Valley, from Stockton across the Delta and along Suisun Bay and San Pablo Bay to Richmond, and until 1933 through the tunnel to its ferry at Ferry Point, Point Richmond.
lines.fate_note: From April 23, 1933 the trains ended at Richmond and ran on to Oakland (Time Table No. 68); the line still carries BNSF's freight and, east of Bay Point, the Gold Runner.
lines.notes: Opens with the first through train from Chicago, July 3, 1900 (the county history of 1926, written by a resident of the time); the line had been put in operation for freight on May 1, and the Santa Fe formally took it over on July 17. The San Francisco Call of July 2, 1900 has the story (page 3), still to be read. Under federal control, from August 18, 1918 the trains ran from Richmond to the Southern Pacific's Oakland Pier instead (CRC Decision No. 5642; Time Table No. 44), until the Santa Fe's own ferry came back, on January 9, 1921 by Time Table No. 47, whose cover shows the date put off twice. When its last passenger train ran at Richmond isn't sourced: the timetables show trains in June 1968 and none in May 1971, so it is drawn to 1968. Its trains to Oakland (from 1904 or so) aren't drawn yet.

running.note: Nos. 1 and 2 at Richmond; No. 17 of May 30, 1971 schedules no passenger train.

segments.notes: The Santa Fe's line of 1900, on which the Gold Runner has run since 1974 (as the San Joaquins). The railroad's return puts it in operation on May 1, 1900, but that was for freight: the Railroad Gazette expected through passengers about two months later, and no official source dates the first, so its date is borrowed from the Santa Fe's trains (July 3, 1900, the county history of 1926). Cut where the Gold Runner joins the line west of Bay Point (Port Chicago in 1932). Checked on the 1908-14 sheets from Antioch to Middle River, which draw the Santa Fe where the Gold Runner runs today (review images in docs/screenshots/p2c/traces/).

lines.name: Seventh Street line
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's electric Red Trains from its Oakland ferry pier along Seventh Street, through East Oakland and Melrose, to Dutton Avenue in San Leandro; over the Bay Bridge to San Francisco from 1939.
lines.fate_note: Replaced from March 22, 1941 by Key System buses and an extension of its A trains, which from April 1941 ran over this line's tracks from East 14th Street to Havenscourt.
lines.notes: The Interurban Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific company authorized in 1936 to take over these lines (CRC D28671), ran them until 1941; the day it took over isn't sourced here. Not yet drawn: Melrose to 106th Avenue (Bond, Beck and Blanche Streets and Bancroft Avenue, which the sources name but don't place) and the 1939–41 "Off-Line" connection from the bridge. Electric trains ran from the Oakland Pier to Melrose from December 1911, mixed with steam until December 30, 1911. When they were extended beyond Melrose to Dutton Avenue isn't sourced: the line still ended at Melrose in September 1913, so the Bancroft Avenue stretch, shown with the line's dates, opened later than it appears.

Trains ran counter-clockwise, arriving at the station's east end.

lines.name: Shattuck Avenue line
lines.summary: The Southern Pacific's electric Red Trains from its Oakland ferry pier to North Berkeley, up Adeline Street and Shattuck Avenue and through the Northbrae Tunnel to Thousand Oaks; over the Bay Bridge to San Francisco from 1939.
lines.fate_note: Replaced by Key System buses on July 26, 1941; from August 6, 1941 Key System's F trains ran over its tracks from Dwight Way to Northbrae.
lines.notes: The Interurban Electric Railway, a Southern Pacific company authorized in 1936 to take over these lines (CRC D28671), ran them until 1941; the day it took over isn't sourced here. Through Northbrae to Thousand Oaks by the loop over Solano Avenue from about February 3, 1912, when service was planned to begin (San Francisco Call, February 2, 1912); the day itself isn't confirmed.

segments.name: Oakland Mole
segments.note: Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (3 hand-read points); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (5 hand-read points). The centre of the mole's bundle of tracks, from the ferry slips to the shore at Seventh Street. The 1915 San Francisco sheet, corrected (sf1915-bay), puts the terminal within about 20 m of the 1949 sheet's.

segments.name: Oakland Mole to Sixteenth Street Station
segments.note: Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
segments.method: Joined to sp-oakland-mole at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (4 hand-read points); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (3 hand-read points). The Southern Pacific main line from the mole through the West Oakland yard to Sixteenth Street Station, as the 1949 sheet draws it; the yard's many tracks make the line's exact track uncertain.
segments.notes: The Southern Pacific's main line, shared with its steam trains; its own dates aren't recorded here.

segments.name: Sixteenth Street Station to 26th Street
segments.note: Until the trains moved to the Bay Bridge
segments.method: Joined to sp-mole-16th-st at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (3 hand-read points). Northeast from Sixteenth Street Station to the junction near the foot of 26th Street.

segments.name: Transbay Terminal loop, San Francisco
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco North 1:24,000 (1950) (23 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). The loop as the 1950 sheet draws it ("KEY SYSTEM"): from the approach, north along the west side to the terminal's west end, through the six-track station facing Mission Street, around the east end and back south. Trains ran counter-clockwise, arriving at the station's east end.

segments.name: San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge, lower deck
segments.method: Joined to bbr-sf-loop at its start; then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco North 1:24,000 (1950) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol and fitted straight (RMS 2 m)); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (8 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (6 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). From Rincon Hill across the bridge's lower deck, through the Yerba Buena Island tunnel, to where the tracks left the bridge on its south side at the Oakland end. The 1946-50 sheets draw the bridge, not the tracks on it; the tracks were on the south half of the lower deck.

segments.name: East Bay approach and yards
segments.method: Joined to bbr-bridge at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (6 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). Along the south side of the bridge approach ("KEY SYSTEM" on the 1949 sheet) past the toll plaza to the East Bay yards, where the Key System's and the Interurban's tracks divided.

segments.name: Interurban lead to 26th Street
segments.method: Joined to bbr-east-approach at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (2 hand-read points); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (7 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). The Interurban's double-track lead from the bridge yards east to the Y at 26th Street, where it met the old Southern Pacific main line.

segments.name: 26th Street to 34th Street
segments.method: Joined to sp-16th-st-26th-st at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (2 hand-read points). North by Wood Street to 34th Street.

segments.name: Wood Street, 34th Street to Ninth Street junction
segments.method: Joined to sp-26th-st-34th-st at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (2 hand-read points); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (7 hand-read points). North along the tracks by Wood Street from 34th Street, curving northeast to the junction at Stanford Avenue and Hollis Street (Ninth Street junction), where the 1949 sheet shows the track splitting north (Ninth Street line) and northeast (Stanford Avenue).

segments.name: Stanford Avenue
segments.method: Along today's Stanford Avenue centerline from Hollis Street to Adeline Street (1781 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949). The private right of way ran beside the avenue (on its south side, as the 1949 sheet draws it); drawn on the avenue's centerline.

segments.name: Adeline Street
segments.method: Along today's Adeline Street centerline from Stanford Avenue to Shattuck Avenue (1460 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949). Private right of way along Adeline Street; drawn on the street's centerline.

segments.name: Shattuck Avenue, Adeline Street to Bancroft Way
segments.method: Along today's Shattuck Avenue centerline from Adeline Street to Bancroft Way (875 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949). Paved-in right of way in Shattuck Avenue.

segments.name: Shattuck Avenue, Bancroft Way to Vine Street
segments.method: Along today's Shattuck Avenue centerline from Bancroft Way to Vine Street (1416 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915). In the paved street.

segments.name: Shattuck Avenue to Sutter Street
segments.method: Joined to sp-shattuck-ave-north at its end; then along today's Henry Street centerline from -122.27072,37.88255 to Sutter Street (342 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Richmond 1:24,000 (1949). The sources call this "connecting private right of way" without placing it; drawn along Henry Street, which the 1941 substitute bus used, as a stand-in, and dashed.

segments.name: Sutter Street to Northbrae Station
segments.method: Along today's Sutter Street centerline from Henry Street to Hopkins Street (361 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Richmond 1:24,000 (1949). In Sutter Street.

segments.name: Northbrae Station through the Northbrae Tunnel to The Alameda
segments.method: Along today's Sutter Street centerline from Hopkins Street to Solano Avenue (71 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); then along today's Solano Avenue centerline from Sutter Street to The Alameda (552 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Richmond 1:24,000 (1949). Private right of way from Northbrae Station through the Northbrae Tunnel, which carries Solano Avenue today, to The Alameda.
segments.notes: The 465-ft tunnel under The Circle is part of this segment; drawn as surface for now. Part of the loop to Thousand Oaks, planned to open February 3, 1912 (San Francisco Call, February 2, 1912); its opening isn't confirmed, so it borrows its lines' dates.

segments.name: Solano Avenue, The Alameda to Thousand Oaks Station
segments.method: Along today's Solano Avenue centerline from The Alameda to Colusa Avenue (218 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Richmond 1:24,000 (1949). In Solano Avenue.
segments.notes: Part of the loop to Thousand Oaks, planned to open February 3, 1912 (San Francisco Call, February 2, 1912); its opening isn't confirmed, so it borrows its lines' dates.

lines.name: South Pacific Coast, Alameda to Santa Cruz
lines.summary: A narrow-gauge railroad from the ferry at Alameda across the marshes to Newark, Santa Clara and San José, then up Los Gatos Creek and through the Santa Cruz Mountains to Felton and Santa Cruz.
lines.notes: Leased to the Southern Pacific from July 1, 1887 (Poor's Manual, 1900); standard-gauged later. When its trains ended isn't sourced: the map draws the line to 1900, the last date a source shows it running (decision 20). In 1940 the Southern Pacific still ran two trains a day from Oakland Pier to San José by Newark (CRC Decision 32804). Its branches to Oakland, Centerville, New Almaden and Boulder Creek aren't drawn as lines of their own.

running.note: The Southern Pacific's lines: "South Pac. Coast Ry. (narrow gauge): Alameda to Santa Cruz 77.6" miles, with its ferry from San Francisco to Alameda.

segments.name: Alameda Mole
segments.note: The mole from March 15, 1884; before it, Alameda Point, not placed here.
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (8 hand-read points); then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (8 hand-read points); the sheet corrected by a shift on 3 control points (Yerba Buena Island on the 1949 Oakland West sheet; +74 m E, +213 m N, RMS 44.8 m). The railroad on the south jetty of the estuary's Deep Water Channel, from the ferry terminal to the junction at Alameda's west shore. Filled over by 1949, so traced from 1915.
segments.notes: The South Pacific Coast's mole, opened in 1884; the Southern Pacific's electric trains used it from 1911.

segments.name: West Alameda, from the mole to Central Avenue
segments.method: Joined to sp-alameda-mole at its end; then OpenHistoricalMap way 200223559 (CC0, as of 2026-10-15), which OHM's mappers drew from USGS San Francisco 1895 topographic map, cut from -122.29160,37.78730 and to -122.27688,37.77144; checked on USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1899). OpenHistoricalMap's way, traced from the 1895 San Francisco sheet, cut where it leaves the mole line and where it reaches Central Avenue.
segments.notes: From the mole south across west Alameda to Central Avenue. It opened partly in 1878 (from Alameda Point) and partly in 1884 (to the mole), but where Alameda Point was isn't placed here, so it shows with its line's dates.

segments.name: Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue, Alameda
segments.method: Along today's Central Avenue centerline from Webster Street to Encinal Avenue (1150 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); then along today's Encinal Avenue centerline from Central Avenue to High Street (3102 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949). In Central Avenue and Encinal Avenue.
segments.notes: The South Pacific Coast's main line of 1878 through Alameda; the Southern Pacific's electric trains ran on it from 1911.

segments.name: Alameda to Newark, across San Leandro Bay and by Alvarado
segments.method: Joined to sp-central-encinal at its end; then OpenHistoricalMap ways 200236874, 200223560, 198748559 (CC0, as of 2026-10-15), which OHM's mappers drew from USGS Concord CA 1897 topographic map; USGS Haywards CA 1899 topographic map, cut from -122.23415,37.75623 and to -122.03253,37.52506; checked on USGS San Leandro 1:24,000 (1948) and USGS Niles 1:24,000 (1953). OpenHistoricalMap's ways, traced from the 1895 San Francisco and 1899 Haywards sheets, cut at the end of the Central Avenue segment and where the line joins today's track east of Newark.
segments.notes: Across San Leandro Bay on a trestle and south along the marshes by Alvarado to Newark, where it joins today's track. When it last carried passengers isn't sourced.

segments.name: Newark to Santa Clara, by Alviso
segments.method: GTFS shapes.txt: 6 shapes run by 191 trips, merged (kept where more than 25 m from track already drawn), simplified to 3 m; the stretch between Newark junction and Santa Clara Amtrak (data/present/extensions.json)

lines.name: Southern Pacific, San Ramon branch
lines.summary: Trains from Avon, on the line from Martinez to Tracy, by Concord, Walnut Creek and Danville to San Ramon; by 1934, mixed trains two days a week.
lines.fate_note: The mixed trains, Nos. 444 and 445, were abandoned under the Railroad Commission's order of February 26, 1934 (Decision No. 26834); the branch went on carrying freight "as necessity demands".
lines.notes: Opened for public use June 7, 1891 (the Railroad Commissioners' report of 1894). Its end is the month of the order that let the Southern Pacific abandon the branch's mixed trains, which required ten days' notice to the public, so the last trains ran in March 1934 at the earliest; the last run isn't dated. The branch was later extended south of San Ramon; that stretch isn't drawn, since the order names only Avon to San Ramon.

segments.name: Avon to Galindo, north of Concord
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS Vine Hill 1:24,000 (1959) (16 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then traced by eye from USGS Vine Hill 1:24,000 (1959) (13 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then traced by eye from USGS Walnut Creek 1:24,000 (1949) (18 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then joined to sp-sr-galindo-danville at its start. Traced from the 1959 Vine Hill sheet, which today's track at Avon checks, and the 1949 Walnut Creek sheet: OpenHistoricalMap's way here, from the 1896 Carquinez Strait sheet, is up to 150 m off.
segments.notes: The branch left the line from Martinez to Tracy at Avon.

segments.name: Galindo to Danville, by Concord and Walnut Creek
segments.method: OpenHistoricalMap way 200221523 (CC0, as of 2026-10-15), which OHM's mappers drew from USGS Concord CA 1897 topographic map, cut from -122.04211,37.98064; checked on USGS Walnut Creek 1:24,000 (1949) and USGS Las Trampas Ridge 1:24,000 (1947). OpenHistoricalMap's way, traced from the 1897 Concord sheet, from where it meets the railroad on the 1949 sheet; within about 10 m of it on the 1947-49 sheets.
segments.notes: South through Concord and Walnut Creek, beside the Sacramento Northern's line for part of the way.

segments.name: Danville to San Ramon
segments.method: OpenHistoricalMap way 200223279 (CC0, as of 2026-10-15), which OHM's mappers drew from USGS Mt Diablo CA 1896 topographic map; checked on USGS Diablo 1:24,000 (1953) and USGS Mt Diablo 1:62,500 (1898). segments.notes: Its end of 1891 at San Ramon, where the 1898 sheet ends the track; it was later extended south (not drawn).

lines.summary: From Poplar Junction down Poplar Street and along 12th Street into downtown Oakland; later out to East Oakland, cut back to 12th and Oak Streets in 1950.
lines.notes: Not yet drawn: the line east of Oak Street to First Avenue and East 14th Street, and its 1941–50 extension to Havenscourt. The day of the 1950 cutback (October 29) is given only by later sources. The last trains ran in 1958 (HAER); April 19 or 20, 1958 is given only by later sources.

segments.name: Key Route Pier
segments.note: Ferry trains, until the Bay Bridge opened to trains
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol and fitted straight (RMS 3 m)); then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (4 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); the sheet corrected by a shift on 3 control points (Yerba Buena Island on the 1949 Oakland West sheet; +74 m E, +213 m N, RMS 44.8 m). The trestle runs straight from the shore, then curves to the ferry terminal.
segments.notes: Ferry trains ran to its end until the Bay Bridge opened to trains in January 1939; from then its land end carried the bridge trains. A 1933 fire is relayed via Wikipedia only.

segments.name: Transbay Terminal loop, San Francisco
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco North 1:24,000 (1950) (23 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). The loop as the 1950 sheet draws it ("KEY SYSTEM"): from the approach, north along the west side to the terminal's west end, through the six-track station facing Mission Street, around the east end and back south. Trains ran counter-clockwise, arriving at the station's east end.

segments.name: San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge, lower deck
segments.method: Joined to bbr-sf-loop at its start; then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco North 1:24,000 (1950) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol and fitted straight (RMS 2 m)); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (8 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (6 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). From Rincon Hill across the bridge's lower deck, through the Yerba Buena Island tunnel, to where the tracks left the bridge on its south side at the Oakland end. The 1946-50 sheets draw the bridge, not the tracks on it; the tracks were on the south half of the lower deck.

segments.name: East Bay approach and yards
segments.method: Joined to bbr-bridge at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (6 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). Along the south side of the bridge approach ("KEY SYSTEM" on the 1949 sheet) past the toll plaza to the East Bay yards, where the Key System's and the Interurban's tracks divided.

segments.name: East Bay yards to the old pier line
segments.method: Joined to bbr-east-approach at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (2 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then joined to key-pier at its start. From the East Bay yards over the bridge approach to the north side of the mole ("TRANSIT LINES" on the 1949 sheet), meeting the old pier line.

segments.name: Pier approach and subway to Poplar Junction
segments.method: Joined to key-pier at its start; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (3 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol); then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (4 hand-read points, centred on the line symbol). segments.name: Poplar Junction to West Grand Avenue
segments.method: Joined to key-trunk-shore at its end; then given point by point; then along today's Poplar Street centerline from -122.28469,37.82298 to West Grand Avenue (774 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1). segments.method: Along today's Poplar Street centerline from West Grand Avenue to 12th Street (893 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1, across gaps of up to 250 m where the street is cut today); checked on USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949). Along Poplar Street.

lines.name: Webster Street line
lines.summary: Southern Pacific electric trains from 14th and Franklin Streets in Oakland down Webster Street and over the Harrison Street swing bridge to Alameda and the Alameda Mole.
lines.notes: Across the estuary by the Harrison Street swing bridge (CRC Decision 17743, not the Webster Street bridge), then, as the 1915 USGS sheet draws the railroad, west along Alameda's north shore to the mole and Alameda Pier; where Webster Junction stood isn't placed. An Oakland Tribune headline of December 26, 1923, "S.P. Bridge Service to End Tonight", relayed by Wikipedia, isn't checked.

segments.name: 14th Street, Franklin Street to Webster Street
segments.method: Along today's 14th Street centerline from Franklin Street to Webster Street (116 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949). In 14th Street.

segments.name: Webster Street, 14th Street to 2nd Street
segments.method: Along today's Webster Street centerline from 14th Street to 2nd Street (1025 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949). In Webster Street.
segments.notes: Single track in 1914; the Webster Street line to 1923 and the Eighteenth Street line from 1926.

segments.name: Webster Street, 2nd Street to 1st Street
segments.method: Along today's Webster Street centerline from 2nd Street to Embarcadero West (92 m; Overture 2026-09-23.1); checked on USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949). In Webster Street, to 1st Street, today's Embarcadero West.
segments.notes: Single track to First Street in 1914, toward the Harrison Street swing bridge.

segments.name: Harrison Street swing bridge across the estuary
segments.method: Joined to sp-webster-2nd-1st at its end; then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (5 hand-read points); the sheet corrected by a shift on 3 control points (Yerba Buena Island on the 1949 Oakland West sheet; +74 m E, +213 m N, RMS 44.8 m). The railroad bridge the 1915 sheet draws across the estuary at the foot of Oakland's street grid; it was gone by 1949.
segments.notes: The sources name the Harrison Street swing bridge; it is traced where the 1915 USGS sheet draws the railroad bridge at the foot of Oakland's street grid, corrected by the sheet's fit near Yerba Buena Island (as the pilot's Alameda Mole), so it carries an error of about 80 m. The Posey Tube replaced the crossing by 1949.

segments.name: Alameda's north shore, the bridge to the mole line
segments.method: Joined to sp-harrison-st-bridge at its end; then traced by eye from USGS Oakland West 1:24,000 (1949) (9 hand-read points); then joined to sp-alameda-mole at its end. The railroad along Alameda's north shore, which the 1949 sheet still draws, west to the mole line.
segments.notes: The sources name the bridge and the pier, not the track between; it is drawn along the railroad on Alameda's north shore, which both the 1915 and 1949 USGS sheets draw from the bridge west toward the mole.

segments.name: Alameda Mole
segments.note: To Alameda Pier and its ferries
segments.method: Traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (8 hand-read points); then traced by eye from USGS San Francisco 1:62,500 (1915) (8 hand-read points); the sheet corrected by a shift on 3 control points (Yerba Buena Island on the 1949 Oakland West sheet; +74 m E, +213 m N, RMS 44.8 m). The railroad on the south jetty of the estuary's Deep Water Channel, from the ferry terminal to the junction at Alameda's west shore. Filled over by 1949, so traced from 1915.
segments.notes: The South Pacific Coast's mole, opened in 1884; the Southern Pacific's electric trains used it from 1911.

segments.name: Bay Point to Stockton, by Antioch and Middle River
segments.method: GTFS shapes.txt: 2 shapes run by 10 trips, merged (kept where more than 25 m from track already drawn), simplified to 3 m; the stretch between Bay Point junction and Stockton, CA San Joaquin Street Station (data/present/extensions.json)
segments.notes: The Santa Fe's line of 1900, on which the Gold Runner has run since 1974 (as the San Joaquins). The railroad's return puts it in operation on May 1, 1900, but that was for freight: the Railroad Gazette expected through passengers about two months later, and no official source dates the first, so its date is borrowed from the Santa Fe's trains (July 3, 1900, the county history of 1926). Cut where the Gold Runner joins the line west of Bay Point (Port Chicago in 1932). Checked on the 1908-14 sheets from Antioch to Middle River, which draw the Santa Fe where the Gold Runner runs today (review images in docs/screenshots/p2c/traces/).

lines.name: SMART
lines.notes: SMART began on August 25, 2017 between the Sonoma County Airport and San Rafael. Its track is older: the San Francisco & North Pacific's of 1870-79 and the line to Tiburon of 1885, dated here stretch by stretch for the past era, as Caltrain's is.

segments.name: Sonoma County Airport to Windsor
segments.note: MTC, May 30, 2025: "Passenger service to the new Windsor station started over the weekend"; only the month is given.
segments.method: GTFS shapes.txt: 2 shapes run by 72 trips, merged (kept where more than 25 m from track already drawn), simplified to 3 m; the stretch between SMART Sonoma County Airport and SMART Windsor (data/present/extensions.json)
segments.notes: The San Francisco & North Pacific's line to Windsor, opened in 1871. SMART's trains reached Windsor in May 2025: MTC's post is dated Friday, May 30, 2025, so which weekend it means isn't clear; only the month is given.

segments.name: Santa Rosa to Sonoma County Airport
segments.method: GTFS shapes.txt: 2 shapes run by 72 trips, merged (kept where more than 25 m from track already drawn), simplified to 3 m; the stretch between SMART Santa Rosa Downtown and SMART Sonoma County Airport (data/present/extensions.json)
segments.notes: The San Francisco & North Pacific's line from Santa Rosa to Windsor, opened in 1871; SMART has run on it since 2017.

segments.name: Petaluma to Santa Rosa
segments.method: GTFS shapes.txt: 2 shapes run by 72 trips, merged (kept where more than 25 m from track already drawn), simplified to 3 m; the stretch between SMART Petaluma Downtown and SMART Santa Rosa Downtown (data/present/extensions.json)
segments.notes: The San Francisco & North Pacific's line of 1870; SMART has run on it since 2017. The company's own returns date it January 1, 1870, before its building in the autumn of 1870 as the county history tells it, so the map takes the history's October 1870.

segments.name: San Rafael to Petaluma
segments.method: GTFS shapes.txt: 2 shapes run by 72 trips, merged (kept where more than 25 m from track already drawn), simplified to 3 m; the stretch between San Rafael Transit Center and SMART Petaluma Downtown (data/present/extensions.json)
segments.notes: The San Francisco & North Pacific's Petaluma branch of 1879, from San Rafael; SMART has run on it since 2017. The branch met the line from Donahue at a junction near Petaluma (Poor's Manual, 1887), so the last stretch into Petaluma may be older. Through Petaluma, OpenHistoricalMap's tracing of the 1914 sheet runs up to 140 m from today's track.

segments.name: San Rafael to Larkspur
segments.note: The Holiday Express of Saturday, December 14, 2019, "marking the official start of passenger service to the new Novato Downtown and Larkspur stations" (SMART's general manager's report, December 2019).
segments.method: GTFS shapes.txt: 2 shapes run by 72 trips, merged (kept where more than 25 m from track already drawn), simplified to 3 m; the stretch between San Rafael Transit Center and SMART Larkspur (data/present/extensions.json)
segments.notes: The line from San Rafael to Tiburon of 1885, through the Cal Park Hill tunnel, which the San Francisco & North Pacific leased as part of its main line (the Commissioners' report, p. 16); OpenHistoricalMap's tracing of the 1897 sheet places it within about 30 m of today's track. SMART's trains reached Larkspur on December 14, 2019.
